planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in sharply drained, gritty, average soil in full sun to light shade in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; azure grape hyacinth needs excellent drainage and a dry summer rest, so avoid heavy, poorly drained sites.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained, average soil in full sun to light shade in fall; azure grape hyacinth is the earliest of the commonly grown muscari to flower, often opening in late February or March ahead of M. armeniacum. Unlike the tight, urn-shaped florets of most grape hyacinths, its short, dense, conical racemes are made up of open, bell-shaped flowers that emerge deep azure-blue from the bud and fade to a paler, almost silvery blue toward the base, giving each spike a soft two-tone gradient. Native to alpine meadows of northeastern Turkey, it is smaller and less vigorously spreading than M. armeniacum, making it well suited to rock gardens, troughs, and the front of a border rather than large-scale naturalizing. A dry summer dormancy is essential for long-term persistence, so it performs best in fast-draining, lean soils rather than rich garden beds.

common_name: Fantasy Creation Grape Hyacinth (Double-Flowered Novelty Muscari)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Fantasy Creation is a naturally occurring double-flowered sport of 'Blue Spike' grown for its unusual, textured, torch-like flower spikes rather than a typical grape-hyacinth silhouette.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Fantasy Creation produces a large, congested, pyramidal raceme of heavily doubled, highly textured florets that give the spike an unusual, almost broccoli-like appearance quite unlike any other grape hyacinth. Color shifts as the flowers age, opening deep blue-purple and fading through lilac to a soft yellow-green by the end of the bloom period, so a single spike shows several tones at once. Because it rarely sets viable seed and the sterile double florets hold their shape rather than collapsing, cut spikes dry well and keep their form in arrangements. Give it the same fall planting and full sun to light shade conditions as other grape hyacinths, and expect a longer-than-average bloom period compared to single-flowered muscari.

common_name: White Striped Squill (Pure White Lebanon Squill)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 3 inches apart in well-drained, average to humus-rich soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; this pure white selection is as easy, hardy, and long-lived as the typical striped blue form and pairs well with it in mixed drifts.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich to average soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for very early spring bloom; this is a clear white-flowered form of striped squill, lacking the faint central blue-grey pencil stripe that gives the typical species its common name, instead bearing clean, unmarked white bells held in the same stiffly upright, densely packed spikes. It blooms at the same very early season as the species, typically alongside snowdrops and Scilla siberica, and shares its parent's exceptional cold hardiness and tolerance of a wide range of soils. Because it is a true-breeding white form rather than a hybrid, it naturalizes reliably from offsets over time, and looks especially effective planted in drifts with the blue-striped species or with early blue Scilla for a two-tone spring carpet. Thrives under deciduous trees and shrubs, receiving full spring sun before the canopy closes overhead.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 4 inches apart in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Dalmatian squill blooms noticeably later than Scilla siberica or S. bifolia, extending the squill season into late spring.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fertile, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for late-spring bloom; Dalmatian squill, native to damp meadows of the Balkan coast, produces dense, conical racemes of small, amethyst-violet, star-shaped flowers on sturdy stems well above the narrow, strappy foliage. It flowers considerably later than the earlier-blooming Siberian and two-leaf squills, typically in May, helping bridge the gap between the earliest spring bulbs and late-spring perennials. Unlike the rapidly self-seeding Siberian squill, it increases more slowly and predictably by offsets, forming tidy, long-lived clumps rather than sweeping colonies, which makes it a good choice for mixed borders or meadow plantings where less aggressive spread is preferred. It tolerates both regular garden moisture and periodic dryness once established, and is largely ignored by deer and rodents.

common_name: Alberto Castillo Spring Starflower (Large White Fragrant Ipheion)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Alberto Castillo is a vigorous, large-flowered white selection found growing in an old Buenos Aires garden and tolerates more sun than the species.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Alberto Castillo bears noticeably larger, pure white, star-shaped flowers than the typical lavender-blue species, each petal marked with only a faint green central stripe, and carries a light violet-like fragrance on mild days. It is more vigorous and sun-tolerant than most ipheion selections, naturalizing readily into broad, dense clumps of narrow, onion-scented, grass-like foliage that emerges in fall and persists through winter. Bloom is heaviest in early to mid-spring, with flowers opening in succession over several weeks. Its onion-scented foliage deters deer and rodents, and it tolerates the dry summer dormancy typical of the genus once established, making it a low-maintenance choice for borders, rock gardens, and naturalized plantings.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Charlotte Bishop arose as a chance seedling of 'Wisley Blue' and is the standard pink-flowered ipheion in cultivation, holding an RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Charlotte Bishop is the classic pink-flowered spring starflower, producing lightly fragrant, star-shaped blooms that range from pale pastel pink to a deeper rose, each petal marked with a darker pink line down its center. Flowers are held just above narrow, onion-scented, grass-like foliage and open over an extended period from mid to late spring. It shares the easy-care nature of the species and other ipheion cultivars, naturalizing steadily by offsets into dense clumps without becoming aggressive, and tolerates dry summer dormancy once established. Its pink tone is a useful departure from the blue and white shades typical of the genus, pairing well with white or blue-flowered ipheion, muscari, or early species tulips in mixed spring plantings.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep and 6-8 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; giant star-of-Bethlehem is a well-behaved clumping bulb, unlike the aggressively spreading common star-of-Bethlehem, O. umbellatum.

directions: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for late-spring bloom; giant star-of-Bethlehem sends up sturdy, upright stems topped with a large, conical-pyramidal raceme densely packed with fragrant, star-shaped white flowers that open in succession from the base upward, extending the display over several weeks. Native to the Caucasus region of Georgia, it is considerably taller and more architectural than common star-of-Bethlehem and, importantly, increases at a modest, well-mannered pace by offsets rather than spreading aggressively, making it a much better choice for mixed borders. The long, sturdy stems and long vase life make it an excellent cut flower, prized by florists and home gardeners alike. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas frequented by pets or small children.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep and 8-10 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed for mid to late summer bloom; in zones below 8, lift bulbs in fall after foliage yellows and store frost-free over winter like gladiolus.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost for mid to late summer bloom; giant chincherinchee is a bold, warm-season bulb native to the grasslands of South Africa and Eswatini, sending up a tall, sturdy flower spike topped with a broad, flattened cluster of large, pristine white, star-shaped flowers, each centered with a striking, glossy deep green to black ovary that gives the blooms real presence at a distance. It flowers well into summer, later than nearly all other commonly grown ornithogalums, and the long-lasting cut flowers are a florist favorite for their dramatic size and remarkable vase life. Unlike the hardy spring-blooming ornithogalums, it is tender and grown much like a gladiolus or dahlia outside of zone 8-10 — planted after the soil has warmed in spring and lifted for winter storage once foliage yellows in fall. All parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in well-drained, average soil in full sun in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Narbonne star-of-Bethlehem is a Mediterranean species that prefers a dry summer rest and lean, fast-draining soil.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun in fall for late-spring bloom; Narbonne star-of-Bethlehem produces slender, narrowly pyramidal racemes packed with 25 to 75 small, milky-white, star-shaped flowers, each petal marked with a fine pale-green central vein, above narrow, fleshy, grey-green leaves. Native to open fields, scrub, and grassland across the Mediterranean basin, it is intermediate in stature between the low-growing common star-of-Bethlehem and the much taller O. magnum, and its tapering, upright racemes give it a more refined, formal silhouette than either. It is more heat- and drought-tolerant than the hardier northern species in this genus, needing a warm, dry summer dormancy to perform reliably from year to year, and is best suited to lean, sharply drained soils in full sun rather than rich, moisture-retentive garden beds.
